title: Huawei Debuts LogicFolding Chip as TSMC, Intel and Samsung Race on ASML's High-NA EUV
subhead: Huawei shipped its first commercial LogicFolding processor, a packaging workaround for US export controls, on the same day TSMC, Intel and Samsung staked out their timelines for ASML's most advanced lithography tool. The two fronts of the chip race — China's architectural improvisation and the West's leading-edge scaling — moved in parallel.

sections.heading: Huawei's LogicFolding Chip Goes Commercial
sections.body: Huawei launched the Kirin 9050 Pro, the first commercial chip using its LogicFolding architecture, powering the new Mate XT 2 trifold smartphone, according to the South China Morning Post. The company says the chip delivers a 42 per cent leap in overall performance over its predecessor alongside improved power efficiency. LogicFolding splits core computing functions across two active silicon layers designed to operate as a single unit — a departure from conventional 3D stacking, which layers largely self-contained dies. The approach is a direct response to US export controls that block Huawei from the world's most advanced lithography equipment. 'LogicFolding is first and foremost a compensatory route — a choice born of external constraints,' Leslie Wu, CEO of semiconductor consultancy RHCC, told SCMP, noting that bonding two active layers adds complex manufacturing steps that can weigh on yields.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first real-world test of whether advanced packaging can substitute for leading-edge lithography at scale. If yields hold, it signals China can keep advancing its most capable chips without access to EUV — narrowing the practical gap that export controls were designed to widen.

sections.heading: The High-NA EUV Race: TSMC, Intel and Samsung Stake Out Timelines
sections.body: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. said it will begin using ASML's high-NA EUV lithography machines from 2030, while Samsung is targeting adoption as early as 2028 and Intel said it is already mass producing with the new tool, Nikkei Asia reports. High-NA EUV is the most advanced chipmaking tool in the world and the next step beyond the EUV systems that already underpin leading-edge production. The divergent timelines reflect each foundry's bet on when the technology becomes cost-effective at volume, with TSMC historically the most conservative adopter of new ASML tools.
sections.whyItMatters: The high-NA EUV race is the leading-edge counterpoint to Huawei's packaging workaround. Whoever masters this tool first extends the performance gap that China is trying to close by other means — and ASML's near-monopoly on it keeps the Netherlands at the center of the chip geopolitics map.

sections.heading: Samsung Opens Japan AI Chip Packaging Hub
sections.body: Samsung Electronics opened an AI chip packaging research center in Yokohama on Tuesday, built with Japanese government aid, to work more closely with Japanese suppliers that dominate back-end chipmaking processes like packaging equipment and materials, Nikkei Asia reports. Samsung's Jun Young-hyun appeared with leaders of Japanese suppliers to open the lab, which aims to speed technology collaboration between South Korea and Japan. The move deepens a Japan-South Korea semiconductor partnership that has been building as both countries seek to reduce dependence on a concentrated supply chain.
sections.whyItMatters: Advanced packaging has become a strategic bottleneck in its own right, and Japan holds much of the materials and equipment expertise. Samsung's decision to co-locate R&D in Japan signals that packaging — not just lithography — is now a front in the competition for AI chip supply-chain security.

sections.heading: China Targets Fourfold Boost in AI Computing Capacity by 2030
sections.body: China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), in a five-year industry plan released Monday, set a target of 9,800 eflops of intelligent computing capacity by 2030 and called for 3.8 trillion yuan (US$532 billion) in cumulative information infrastructure investment over 2026-2030, the South China Morning Post reports. The plan calls for the 'orderly deployment' of intelligent computing clusters with 10,000 or 100,000-plus GPU cards and for adapting infrastructure to home-grown computing chips. China's intelligent computing capacity reached 2,185 eflops by the end of June, up 177 per cent year-on-year, with 52 facilities each equipped with more than 10,000 accelerator cards. The target means China would need to more than quadruple the June level. The buildout extends the 'East Data, West Computing' project launched in 2022.
sections.whyItMatters: The scale of the target — and the explicit push to adapt infrastructure to domestic chips — shows Beijing is treating AI compute as national infrastructure, not just a commercial market. The 177 per cent year-on-year growth also suggests China's compute buildout is accelerating even under US export controls on advanced processors.

sections.heading: G7 Urges Industry to Speed Up Post-Quantum Encryption
sections.body: A cybersecurity working group at the G7 is urging governments and industry to accelerate defenses against quantum computers that could break existing public-key encryption, CyberScoop reports. The working group's report, prepared in June at the G7 Summit in France, said organizations 'can no longer afford to postpone' transitioning critical systems to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). It warned that the quantum threat 'remains off the radar for many organizations and not properly resourced,' and that leaders 'must reframe the quantum threat from a distant future problem to a near-term threat.' The report flagged that 'harvest now, decrypt later' attacks — collecting encrypted data today to decrypt it once quantum computers mature — are a present-day risk.
sections.whyItMatters: The G7's collective push signals that post-quantum migration is moving from a technical exercise to a policy deadline. For governments and critical-infrastructure operators, the window to inventory and re-encrypt systems is closing, and the cost of delay is measured in data that may already be compromised.

sections.heading: Sality Botnet Dismantled After 23-Year Run
sections.body: Law enforcement, CrowdStrike and the Shadowserver Foundation dismantled Sality, a Russia-based botnet that infected more than 11 million devices over a 23-year run, CyberScoop reports. The peer-to-peer botnet evaded disruption for so long because it lacked centralized architecture. CrowdStrike said it targeted Sality's peer list of infected machines and tricked the network into permanently cutting off access to those devices. Sality's domains were seized in a coordinated effort supported by the FBI, the Justice Department, Europol, and authorities from Bulgaria, Hungary and Romania. CrowdStrike attributed three DDoS attacks to Sality, suggesting the operator was occasionally willing to use the botnet for political aims, though it was primarily financially motivated.
sections.whyItMatters: The takedown is a notable win against decentralized, peer-to-peer botnet infrastructure that has long been considered hard to disrupt. It also shows the growing role of private-sector firms like CrowdStrike working alongside law enforcement in dismantling state-adjacent criminal infrastructure.

sections.heading: Pegasus and NoviSpy Found on Serbian Activists' Devices
sections.body: Researchers uncovered the first confirmed Pegasus spyware infection of 2026, along with a new NoviSpy variant, targeting Serbian student activists and others, CyberScoop reports. The SHARE Foundation said it found 14 people targeted, including a member of parliament and a local government official. The University of Toronto's Citizen Lab confirmed the Pegasus infection of a student activist with 'high probability,' while Amnesty International confirmed two devices had been infected with a new NoviSpy version. The infections coincided with the build-up to local elections in March and ahead of October parliamentary elections, with student protests rising after the 2024 Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse. SHARE called it the largest documented wave of such surveillance in Serbia to date.
sections.whyItMatters: The case shows commercial spyware remains a live tool of political surveillance in Europe, not just in authoritarian states. The confirmed Pegasus infection — the first of 2026 — and the new NoviSpy variant underscore how quickly spyware vendors iterate, and how hard it is for civil society to detect and respond.

bottomLine: Today the chip race moved on two fronts at once. Huawei shipped its first commercial LogicFolding processor, testing whether advanced packaging can substitute for the leading-edge lithography that US export controls deny it, while TSMC, Intel and Samsung staked out their timelines for ASML's high-NA EUV tool — the technology that defines the performance gap China is trying to close. In parallel, China's MIIT set a fourfold AI-compute target for 2030, the G7 pushed industry to accelerate post-quantum encryption, and law enforcement dismantled the 23-year-old Sality botnet. The through-line is that compute — its hardware, its security, and its control — remains the central terrain of tech geopolitics, with both the US-led bloc and China investing heavily to shape who gets to build and use the most advanced systems.
sources: South China Morning Post, Nikkei Asia, CyberScoop
